source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Founding modern test. One 30-minute video or one 60-minute computer game cut bias on three biases, and the effect lasted months. The game, with personal feedback and practice, beat the passive video.
numbers: Exp 1 (bias blind spot, confirmation bias, fundamental attribution error): 243 completed lab (game n=160, video n=83), 196 did online follow-up at 8 weeks (game 130, video 66). Overall bias fell 46.25% (game) and 18.60% (video) at once; 34.76% and 20.10% at follow-up. Overall d pre-post: game 1.68, video 0.69; pre-follow-up: game 1.11, video 0.66.
limits: No passive no-training control group; design is pre/post with game vs video, so test-retest and demand effects are not separated. Paid convenience sample in Pittsburgh (mean age 24.5). Bias scales built by the authors.
agent_relevance: Training that gives feedback on the learner's own errors and more practice beats explanation alone. For an agent: a stored lesson with graded worked feedback on its own past misses may beat a warning in the prompt.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Experiment 2 on anchoring, projection (social projection) and representativeness. Game and video were about equal on anchoring and representativeness; game was better on projection. The game added adaptive practice.
numbers: 238 completed (game n=156, video n=82); 192 did follow-up at 12 weeks (game 126, video 66). Overall bias fell 31.94% (game) and 25.70% (video) at once; 23.57% and 19.20% at follow-up. Overall d pre-post: game 1.74, video 1.75; pre-follow-up game 1.16, video 1.07. Game vs video: better at once F(1,235)=13.44, p<.001; at 3 months only marginal p=.057. Anchoring d: game .70/.63, video .80/.66 (no difference). Projection d: game 1.11/.54, video .49/.14. Representativeness d: game 1.51/1.05, video 1.80/1.09.
limits: The feedback advantage is not universal: for anchoring and representativeness the passive video did as well. Still no passive control. Effects measured on the authors' own scales.
agent_relevance: The gain from feedback depends on the bias. Do not assume one training format works for all biases; test per bias.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Transfer inside a bias: the game lowered confirmation bias on facets it did not teach, though less than on taught facets at first.
numbers: Confirmation bias: six facets, game taught three. Untrained facets fell at posttest t(159)=10.05, d=.79 and follow-up t(129)=7.42, d=.65. Taught vs untrained facets at posttest: t(159)=2.56, p<.05, d=.20; no difference at follow-up.
limits: Transfer is to other items of the same bias, not to other biases. The paper says effects were 'domain-general' across contexts of the same bias.
agent_relevance: Lessons should state the abstract rule of a bias, not one example. Near transfer (same bias, new surface) is plausible; far transfer is not shown here.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Knowledge of biases and reduced bias are different things. The video taught bias recognition better than the game at once, but the game debiased more in Exp 1.
numbers: Bias knowledge (0-100), Exp 2: game 35.89 pre, 63.16 post, 50.65 follow-up; video 39.03 pre, 74.11 post, 52.04 follow-up (d=1.53 post). Video beat game on knowledge at once, F(1,235)=11.07, p<.001; equal by follow-up. Exp 1 game knowledge 35.78 pre, higher post.
limits: Knowledge scale is recognition and discrimination of bias examples, not behaviour in a live decision.
agent_relevance: Telling the model what a bias is (declarative lesson) is not the same as removing it. Check the behaviour, not the knowledge, as the pass test (matches G3).

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: The paper lists Fischhoff's four training procedures and says the game used all four, the video only the first two plus mitigation tips.
numbers: (1) teach each bias, (2) teach its direction of influence, (3) give feedback, (4) extended feedback with coaching, intervention and mitigation strategies. Video: about 30 min; game: about 60 min. Game had 5 confirmation-bias practice judgments with immediate feedback (Exp 1) and up to 16 adaptive practice questions (Exp 2).
quote: teaching people about each bias, teaching people the directional influence of each bias on judgment, providing feedback
limits: The paper does not isolate which of the four ingredients caused the gain: it says more research is needed to determine why the game worked better.
agent_relevance: Maps to a schema lesson with four parts: name the bias, say which way it pushes, show feedback on a real miss, add coached correction. We cannot yet say which part carries the gain.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: The same paper's literature summary: evidence that training improves general decision making was inconclusive; experts fail to transfer; strategies that add neglected information or teach rules show promise; large-dose statistical coursework works.
numbers: Cites: philosophers trained in logic show the same moral preference reversals (Schwitzgebel and Cushman 2012); physicians show survival/mortality framing reversals (McNeil et al. 1982); weather forecasters are calibrated in domain but overconfident on general knowledge (Murphy and Winkler 1974; Wagenaar and Keren 1986).
quote: Evidence that training effectively improves general decision making ability is inconclusive at present
limits: This is the authors' framing of earlier work, written by the team that built the games; read as context, not as independent review.
agent_relevance: Domain training does not spread to new domains unless the learner can see the underlying structure. This is the central risk for lesson libraries: lessons must be indexed by problem structure.

source: Nisbett, Fong, Lehman and Cheng (1987) Teaching reasoning, Science 238:625-631
finding: Reported in secondary summaries and in Morewedge 2015: brief formal training in statistical rules raised use of those rules in everyday-event reasoning; graduate study in law, medicine and psychology raised statistical and methodological reasoning, while chemistry did not and logic courses did not raise the logic tests used.
numbers: Not opened. Search summary: all three intervention groups beat control on abstract statistical rule use in new situations. Morewedge 2015 says statistical coursework and graduate training in psychology and medicine increase use of statistics and logic in everyday problems. Exact N and effect sizes not recorded: not read.
limits: Full paper not read this session (Science paywall). Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Probabilistic and statistical rules can be taught and used outside the classroom, but only in fields that practise them. For the agent: rules are best attached to the kind of problem where they apply.

source: Fischhoff (1982) Debiasing, in Kahneman, Slovic and Tversky (eds), Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases
finding: Founding review of debiasing. Morewedge 2015 describes it as the source of the four-step training taxonomy and calls the field's start rocky. Its warning result (warning alone gives little or no reduction) is known from the literature but was not read.
numbers: Not opened. Only the Morewedge 2015 description of its four procedures is known (see a05).
limits: Not read. Book chapter with no open copy found.
agent_relevance: Origin of the claim that warnings alone fail and that feedback and coaching are needed. Our rules already treat warnings as weak; this is the human root.

source: Hirt and Markman (1995) Multiple explanation: a consider-an-alternative strategy for debiasing judgments, JPSP 69:1069-1086
finding: Consider-an-alternative: asking people to explain more than one possible outcome reduces bias in judgments. Morewedge 2015 cites it as an example of training that adds information normally under-weighted.
numbers: Not opened. Numbers not recorded: not read.
limits: Not read this session. Whether the benefit needs the alternatives to be generated, not just considered, is not checked here.
agent_relevance: Direct human root of the consider-the-alternative operator. Link to our reframe or alternative-search operator, firing only on signal (G1).

source: Larrick, Morgan and Nisbett (1990) Teaching the use of cost-benefit reasoning in everyday life, Psychological Science 1:362-370
finding: Training in cost-benefit rules led people to follow them in everyday decisions, such as sunk-cost choices. Cited by Morewedge 2015 as teaching normative rules people did not know.
numbers: Not opened. Numbers not recorded: not read.
limits: Not read. Cited only via Morewedge 2015 text.
agent_relevance: A rule taught as a rule can transfer; this supports storing a short normative rule rather than an example.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament, Psychological Science 25:1106-1115
finding: In the IARPA forecasting tournament, probability training, teaming and tracking each improved forecast accuracy, through better calibration and resolution.
numbers: Not opened (PDF fetch returned empty; abstract seen only in search results). Size of the training effect not recorded.
limits: Not read. Training was a short probabilistic reasoning module, not game-based; forecasters had outcome feedback over a season.
agent_relevance: A live example that teaching probability rules plus real outcome feedback improves judgment in a long-run setting. Link to the Good Judgment Project subfield (parallel).

source: Shepperd, Mair and Jorgensen (2018) An experimental evaluation of a de-biasing intervention for professional software developers
finding: A workshop on judgment biases cut, but did not remove, anchoring in professional developers who estimated their project productivity after a low or high anchor.
numbers: 410 developers from several countries in company settings; 292 earlier participants without the workshop pooled with new ones. Anchor effect robust Cohen's d = 1.19; with workshop d = 0.72. Trimmed mean difference 25.6 (95% CI 15.5 to 35.7), mostly on the high anchor. Spread of estimates fell about threefold (20% trimmed SD).
limits: Quasi-experimental: comparison group came from an earlier published study, not random assignment to workshop. Workshop was awareness-only, no feedback practice. True productivity unknown.
agent_relevance: Awareness training alone gave a medium reduction (d from 1.19 to 0.72), not zero. Fits the view that anchors are cut by training but never to zero.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley and He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Builds a 13,465-prompt benchmark for cognitive-bias-like patterns in LLMs (framing, group attribution, anchoring/primacy, status quo) in student admission tasks and tests awareness, contrastive, counterfactual and few-shot mitigations plus a self-help method where the model rewrites its own prompt.
numbers: Framing gap (admit minus reject rate): GPT-4 baseline -0.405 (admits 40.5% more students under the reject frame); self-help -0.010. GPT-3.5 baseline 0.165, self-help -0.080. Group attribution Llama-2-7B: classifies 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Self-help cut biased prompt elements to 0% for group attribution and 2.7% for framing in GPT-4. Awareness prompting gave small, uneven change. Few-shot (contrastive, counterfactual) often caused failures that drove admit/reject rate to 0 or 1.
limits: Models are GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B and 13B; old by 2026. Bias is defined as difference between two framings, not error against ground truth. Admission task is synthetic. Only 400 prompts per experiment for GPT on two biases.
agent_relevance: In an LLM, example-based few-shot debiasing is fragile and can break the answer; a model rewriting its own biased prompt worked best and needs a strong model. Supports G2: revise from a located signal; supports caution about adding bias lessons as long examples.

source: Lyu, Ren, Feng, Wang, Chen, Ren and de Rijke (2025) Self-adaptive cognitive debiasing for LLMs in decision-making (SACD)
finding: SACD loops three steps until no bias is found: determine bias, analyse it, rewrite the prompt. It had the lowest mean bias score across finance (FOMC), healthcare (PubMedQA) and legal (LegalBench) tasks, for anchoring, bandwagon, loss aversion and all three together, on four models.
numbers: FOMC, llama3.1-8b: vanilla mean bias 0.3805; few-shot 0.4215; CoT 0.3425; Reflexion 0.3830; multi-agent debate 0.5020; zero-shot debias 0.2965; few-shot debias 0.2970; self-help 0.2100; SACD 0.1570. SACD range across models and domains 0.03 to 0.179 (FOMC 0.0300-0.1570; PubMedQA 0.0425-0.1790; LegalBench 0.0400-0.1235). Few-shot debiasing often above 0.5, sometimes above 0.8. Self-help was second best (0.0625-0.2625), weaker with several biases (0.2300 on LegalBench llama-8b).
limits: Bias score is shift in choice toward the biased target between treated and control prompts, not accuracy. Authors report the average; significance by model not read in full. Prompt-rewrite method, so it needs the model to detect the bias in the prompt.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a signal-triggered loop: detect, analyse, fix, repeat until clean. Also shows CoT, reflection and debate do not remove bias and debate raised it, matching our G4 and G1.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) SACD, on multi-agent and reflective prompting
finding: Reflexion and multi-agent debate had the highest bias scores, especially with several biases at once, because they learn from biased feedback or other biased agents (authors' explanation).
numbers: Examples: FOMC, gpt-3.5-turbo, multi-agent debate mean bias 0.5155. PubMedQA, llama3.1-70b, Reflexion 0.5585. CoT range 0.2470 to 0.6150 across domains, the best of the generic prompting methods.
limits: Authors' explanation is not tested directly. Closed-weight models gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4o.
agent_relevance: Warns against adding a debate or critic stage and expecting less bias. Backs G4 (no voter personas) and G5 (judge sees no proposed answer).

source: Huang, Bie, Na, Ruan, Lei, Yue and He (2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLM with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Builds SynAnchors for anchoring in LLMs. Anchoring is common, acts in shallow layers, and cannot be removed by conventional strategies; explicit reasoning helps most.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct baseline total anchored ratio 34.7%; Anti-DP (a prompt that sets a standard first, then re-thinks) 24.7%; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse); self-improving 38.4%; adversarial LoRA fine-tuning 33.3%; DoLa 37.5/38.5%. Qwen2.5-7B baseline 40.0%; Anti-DP 40.8%; self-improving 48.0%. Authors: strategies achieved up to 10% alleviation.
limits: Small models (7B and 8B), small test sets; Qwen did not improve with Anti-DP on numeric items. Some strategies made anchoring worse.
agent_relevance: Training the model (adversarial LoRA) did little; a reasoning-first prompt helped on one model. Supports scaffold over training, but the scaffold gain is small and model-specific.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-4o answers shift with low and high anchor hints. Chain-of-thought, thoughts of principles, ignore-the-anchor instructions and reflection gave no significant improvement. Showing both a low and a high hint worked when the two hints bracket the true value.
numbers: 62 questions with three hints each (fact, expert opinion, irrelevant). Both-Anchor strategy tested with GPT-4: answers came close to the bias-free value on the questions where the two hints straddled it (nos. 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15); on the others they still deviated.
limits: Small dataset, two models, no formal effect sizes beyond t-test plots; Both-Anchor only works when the two hints straddle the truth.
agent_relevance: Collect hints from several angles is the same as consider-the-alternative; ignoring the anchor by instruction fails, as human warning studies predict.

source: Sovrano, Dominici and Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating prompt-induced cognitive biases in general-purpose AI for software engineering (PROBE-SWE)
finding: Eight biases (anchoring, availability, bandwagon, confirmation, framing, hindsight, hyperbolic discounting, overconfidence) in software dilemmas. Common prompts such as CoT and self-debiasing gave no significant per-bias reduction. Injecting explicit best-practice rules (axiomatic background self-elicitation) cut bias sensitivity by 51% on average and up to 73% for some biases.
numbers: Models: DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-4.1 Nano, Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B. Axiomatic cues cut overall sensitivity 51% on average (p<.001). CoT degraded results on Llama-3.3-70B. Open-ended outputs tested in a smaller RQ4 on gpt-4o-mini and llama-3.1-8b.
limits: Sensitivity is flip rate between biased and unbiased versions of a dilemma. Not frontier models. Rules are written by the authors per domain.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of statistical-rule training: put the normative rule in view before answering. A rule library per task type beat generic be-unbiased prompts. Link to worked examples subfield (parallel).

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak and An (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Four bias families (judgment, information processing, social, response). Prompt-level debiasing helps a lot on response bias but backfires on judgment bias; the bias is linearly readable in activations and activation steering cut bias 26 to 32%.
numbers: Vanilla baselines (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B): judgment shift 4.3, 7.7, 2.7 pp; first-option selection 79.0, 77.1, 77.6% (chance 36.8%). Debias prompt effect: response position independence +40.5%, social accuracy +5.9%, information processing -1.1%, judgment accuracy -4.4% (backfires). Steering: 26-32% bias reduction; Llama near-zero loss on 25 benchmarks, Qwen up to -19.0 pp on judgment steering.
limits: Pre-print, under review. Judgment-bias metric is an accuracy shift on its own tasks; steering needs open weights and is outside a prompt scaffold.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to be unbiased can make judgment-type biases worse. That is the LLM version of warnings do not work. Use a bias-family-specific tool, not a general debias instruction.

source: Raj, Mansouri, Caliskan, Anastasopoulos and Zhu (2026) Debias It Yourself: teaching LLMs cognitive bias-mitigation interventions (DIY)
finding: Translates five social-psychology prejudice-reduction practices (stereotype replacement, counter-stereotypical imaging, individuation, perspective-taking, positive contact) into step procedures. Delivers them by in-context examples (SHOW), instruction tuning (TRAIN) or guided two-pass self-revision (REVISE). TRAIN plus REVISE and self-revision ranked top.
numbers: Three models, five bias benchmarks, eleven baselines, three reasoning benchmarks. Best configurations reach mean bias as low as 2% at 90% reasoning accuracy and cut bias on unseen dimensions by up to 14.8 pp. On Llama-8B, DIY-TRAIN-REVISE gained +14.98 pp [11.22, 17.26] on the first benchmark while SHOW alone was -2.34 [-5.07, +0.49]. Llama-70B SHOW -8.17 [-10.55, -5.69]; TRAIN-REVISE +14.36.
limits: Social-bias benchmarks (stereotype and fairness), not judgment errors like anchoring. Dimensions were chosen by the authors. Pre-print. Column mapping of the table was read from layout text and may be imprecise.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of train vs show vs revise: showing examples was weak or harmful, a procedure plus a revision pass was strong. For a no-training agent: use the revise pass with a procedure, not examples alone.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) BiasBuster, on few-shot failure
finding: Few-shot debiasing with bias examples can push a model to refuse or accept everything. Authors explain that examples must be tailored to each bias, are long, and may introduce new biases.
numbers: Table 3: Llama-2-7B contrastive admit 0.996, reject 1.000 (flagged as instruction failure, under 1% variation); counterfactual admit 0.542, reject 0.000. Llama-2-13B contrastive admit 0.432, reject 1.000.
limits: Old Llama-2 models. Failure may be model-specific; GPT-4 handled the same prompts more stably.
agent_relevance: A stored worked example can overwhelm the task. Keep lessons short and check that the lesson does not shift the answer when no bias is present.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) SACD, on few-shot debiasing replication
finding: A second group's test across more models agrees with BiasBuster: few-shot debiasing is the weakest family and gives mean bias scores often above 0.5.
numbers: FOMC llama3.1-70b: vanilla 0.1648, few-shot 0.3655 (worse), CoT 0.2220, zero-shot debias 0.1345, few-shot debias 0.2900, self-help 0.1885. Authors cite Echterhoff et al. for the cause: added context changes the prompt.
limits: Metrics differ between papers. Few-shot sometimes helped on other cells.
agent_relevance: Treat example-based lessons as risky until tested on the target model; zero-shot rule statements did better.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) read with the LLM studies: synthesis of the training ingredients
finding: Reading the human game study next to the LLM studies: feedback plus practice on own errors worked in people; in LLMs the working analogues are (a) detect the bias in the actual prompt and rewrite it (SACD, BiasBuster self-help), (b) apply a stated rule or procedure in a revision pass (DIY, PROBE-SWE), while (c) generic be-unbiased or chain-of-thought prompts did little or backfired (CogBias, Lou and Sun, PROBE-SWE).
numbers: Human: game d up to 1.74 overall, shrinking to about 1.1 at 2 to 3 months. LLM: SACD 0.157 vs vanilla 0.3805 mean bias (llama3.1-8b, FOMC); PROBE-SWE axiomatic cues -51%; CogBias prompt debias -4.4% on judgment.
limits: Synthesis by this agent across different metrics; not a pooled estimate. LLM studies are unreplicated pre-prints.
agent_relevance: Design implication: debias only on a located signal, with a short rule and a revision from real output. Lessons should be per bias family. Matches G1, G2 and G5; argues against a generic anti-bias preamble.

source: Raj et al. (2026) DIY, on the human basis (Devine 2012; Galinsky and Moskowitz 2000)
finding: The paper's human basis: Devine et al. (2012) habit-breaking intervention reduced implicit race bias, sustained over time; Galinsky and Moskowitz (2000) showed perspective-taking reduces stereotype expression. The paper says bias falls by changing how information is processed at the moment of encounter, not by suppressing single answers.
numbers: No human numbers given in this paper; cited only. DIY transfer to unseen bias dimensions up to 14.8 pp.
quote: bias is reduced by changing how social information is processed at the moment of encounter
limits: Human claims are second-hand here. Later work on the lasting effect of Devine 2012 was not checked.
agent_relevance: Perspective-taking and counter-example imagining are the human roots of the consider-the-other-side operator. Treat the sustained-change claim as unverified.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) BiasBuster, on self-help needing high capacity
finding: Self-debiasing by having the model re-read all information and revise its own decisions works only for stronger models. Weak models over-correct.
numbers: Llama models changed 40 to 52% of their sequential decisions when asked to debias (Table 4). Authors conclude self-help for anchoring needs high-capacity models.
limits: Llama-2 only; no GPT-4 number on this exact test in the text read.
agent_relevance: Revision with a bias hint can overshoot. Keep a held-out check (G3) so a revision is accepted only when it passes.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) on the human analogue of warnings
finding: Authors note that Simmons et al. also found anchoring hard to remove fully in human experiments, and that telling the model to ignore the anchor did not help GPT-4 or GPT-4o.
numbers: None beyond the significance plots: answers with H2 and H3 hints stayed consistently shifted, with very small p-values, under all four strategies.
limits: Qualitative claim from figures; no table of effect sizes read.
agent_relevance: Instruction to ignore a bias is not a debiasing method. This repeats the human warning result (Fischhoff 1982) in LLMs.
